title: CASE P-29 — the walk that never stands still
intro: Field Recovery was handed a subject, not a place. The file says he can widen the Planck length around his own body, and that when he does, he noclips: out of this room and into the next instance of himself, somewhere across the Tegmark Level I multiverse. The only physical trace anyone has is a 56-page record written in 29 runes, published in 2014 and never read. We did not try to read it. We measured it. Every number below is real and was computed from the public record. The mathematics is the corridor. The answer is always standing in the middle of it, in plain sight. Most people stop reading before they reach it.

stations.title: i · the walk
stations.clue: Treat each rune as a room. The record visits N = 12,956 rooms drawn from an alphabet of 29. First ask whether he favours any room. The index of coincidence is IoC = 29 · Σ nᵢ(nᵢ − 1) / (N(N − 1)), where nᵢ counts visits to room i. English text gives 1.71. A subject with no preference gives 1.000. The record gives .9999. Pearson's statistic against the uniform law, χ² = Σ (nᵢ − N/29)² / (N/29), is 26.4 on twenty-eight degrees of freedom, dead centre of chance. So he has no favourite room. Now ask the only question that matters about a man who is said to noclip: does he ever stay? There are N − 1 = 12,955 consecutive pairs. If each room were chosen independently, the probability that he is in the same room twice running is 1/29, so the expected count of stays is 12,955 / 29 = 446.7 with standard deviation √(12,955 · (1/29)(1 − 1/29)) = 20.8. — STOP HERE. THIS IS THE ANSWER. HE WAS CAUGHT IN THE SAME ROOM TWICE EXACTLY EIGHTY-SIX TIMES. TYPE IT IN DIGITS. — That is 360.7 below expectation, or 17.4 standard deviations: a rate of .66% where chance demands 3.45%. The deficit is strictly lag 1. At lags 2 through 10 the coincidence rate returns to 3.4%–3.7%. It holds inside words (.62%), across word breaks (.81%) and across line breaks (.75%), so it belongs to the walker and not to the page. Each one was re-read from the 2400 × 3600 page scans by nearest-template classification over 8,229 reference glyphs; the reading reproduced 12,930 of 12,956 runes and confirmed every one of those pairs, the weakest by a margin of 4.4 to 1. Whatever wrote this record moves at every step.
stations.prompt: how many times he was caught in the same room twice — digits only

stations.title: ii · the leak
stations.clue: Eighty-six stays is not zero. A perfect noclipper would leave none, so the stays are the sightings, and sightings have a rhythm or they do not. Let g₁ … g₈₅ be the gaps, in rooms, between consecutive stays. For a memoryless process with per-step probability p, the gaps are geometric: mean 1/p, median ln(½)/ln(1 − p), and coefficient of variation σ/μ → 1. Measured: mean 150.8, median 113 against a geometric prediction of 104, coefficient of variation .94. That mean is the whole instrument, because the rate is p = (the count from the first instrument) / 12,955. — READ THIS LINE AND NOTHING ELSE: HE SLIPS ONCE IN EVERY ONE HUNDRED FIFTY-ONE STEPS. TYPE IT IN DIGITS. — Now make sure the slips carry no message. Test for hidden periods by reducing each sighting's position modulo m for every m from 2 to 60 and taking the largest χ² per degree of freedom: m = 9 at 2.07, permutation p = .47. Test whether the sightings prefer a place in the word: initial 23, medial 44, final 19, against 18.7, 48.1 and 18.7 for a process blind to position. Test whether a sighting marks a particular letter of a hidden plaintext: for the rune EA the predicted count is 74, close to the count from the first instrument, but the fit of the positions is −127 in log-likelihood, where a true marker would score +64 ± 8 and blind chance scores −121 ± 20. Blind chance it is. So the slips are random. The exact figure is 1 in 150.6, with a 95% interval from 1 in 125 to 1 in 192. The authors of the record printed a square of numbers on one of their solved pages. One of its entries is 131. Another is this instrument's answer. We record that as a coincidence and do not rely on it.
stations.prompt: he slips once in every how many steps — digits only

stations.title: iii · the step
stations.clue: Define the step Dᵢ = cᵢ − cᵢ₋₁ (mod 29), the displacement from one room to the next. The file's claim is that the subject widens the Planck length around himself, ℓ_P = √(ħG/c³) ≈ 1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ m, the scale below which position stops meaning anything. In tested physics that length is fixed. In several serious theories it is a dial: the value of a field in scalar-tensor gravity, the size of a hidden dimension in braneworld models, the count of light particle species in Dvali's bound, the healing length of a condensate if spacetime is one. Turn the dial and count what is left. The entropy a region can hold is bounded by S ≤ A / (4ℓ_P²). For a sphere of radius 1 m, A = 4π m², and at today's value S ≤ 1.2 × 10⁷⁰ nats, which is why the nearest exact copy of a room is unthinkably far. The observable universe holds 8.5 × 10⁷⁹ such spheres. A copy falls inside it when e^S drops to that number, S = 184 nats, and that happens at ℓ_P = 13 cm. At that width a one-metre region is 265 bits. The price: the Planck mass falls to ħ/(ℓ_P c) = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴² kg, so a single electron would sit inside its own horizon, and widening by brute force destroys the traveller. Whatever the method, in a record it would look like this: a smallest step too large to fit inside one room, a step that is never zero. Excluding the sightings, the steps fall on the nonzero residues, and they fall evenly: χ² = 41.4 on 27 degrees of freedom over the whole record, and page by page the statistic averages 27.5 with standard deviation 7.2, against 27 and 7.3 for perfectly uniform steps. The authors wrote, on a page they let us read: the primes are sacred; the totient function is sacred. Euler's totient φ(n) counts the integers below n that share no factor with n. For a prime it is n − 1. — THE WHOLE STATION IS THIS ONE FACT: φ(29) = TWENTY-EIGHT. THERE ARE TWENTY-EIGHT WAYS TO LEAVE A ROOM AND NO WAY TO STAY. TYPE IT IN DIGITS. — Those residues form the multiplicative group (ℤ/29ℤ)×, cyclic, with φ(φ(29)) = 12 generators. We wrote every step as a power gˣ and added six candidate key streams in the exponent modulo φ(29), for all 12 generators and six restart rules: 432 variants, best coincidence 1.002 where English reads 1.71. We ran the authors' own published method, a shift by φ of the i-th prime, at each of the first 6,000 starting offsets: best 1.003. We encrypted English with each method they ever published and counted stays: 3% to 4.2% every time, never .66%. Repeated strings of three, four and five rooms occur 3,580, 129 and 6 times, against 3,690, 131.8 and 4.7 for a walk with no memory. No key restarts. No state is ever reused. He never takes the same path twice. One mechanism in the literature fits a walker like that without destroying him. In braneworld models ordinary matter is confined to a three-dimensional surface and gravity is not, and a path that leaves the surface and returns elsewhere is called a bulk shortcut. A wall is only a wall for things that stay on the surface. If that is what he does, it can be measured: gravity near him would depart from the inverse-square law, and if the change runs through a warp factor his atomic spectral lines would shift as well. And 265 bits is too few to hold a body. It does not need to hold a body, only a moment. Nobody has measured how many bits one moment of experience requires. The file proposes 266. Run the count again with that number: 2²⁶⁶ possible moments against 8.5 × 10⁷⁹ rooms gives .72 of a copy inside the horizon. One bit fewer and the next instance of him would be somewhere we could look. At 266 it lies about twelve percent past the edge of everything that can be seen. If the file is right, that is why there is a record of his walk and no photograph of the two of them.
stations.prompt: the number of ways to leave a room — digits only

stations.title: iv · the page
stations.clue: The last readable page of the record says that within the deep web there exists a page that hashes to a stated 512-bit value, and that it is the duty of every pilgrim to seek it out. A cryptographic hash H maps any input to 512 bits and cannot be run backwards: finding an input for a given output costs on the order of 2⁵¹² ≈ 1.34 × 10¹⁵⁴ trials. At a billion billion guesses per second that takes about 10¹¹⁸ times the age of the universe. So we searched instead. Six hash functions, three of them written by hand and proven on published test vectors. 1,011 distinct archived files, 1.5 gigabytes. 105,895 lines and addresses. 202,294 candidates built from the record's own numbers. — HERE IS THE ANSWER, AS PLAINLY AS IT CAN BE PUT: THE NUMBER OF PAGES THAT MATCHED IS ZERO. NOT ONE. TYPE THE DIGIT. — Then someone asked the question that closes the file: what if the page is not there to be found, because it is yours to make? Take it with the mathematics of the place. In a spatially infinite universe that is the same everywhere on average, every finite arrangement of matter recurs. A region that can hold at most 10^115 particles has at most 2^(10^115) arrangements, so an exact copy of this room, this file and its reader lies about 10^(10^115) metres away, and another beyond that, without end. The paper on the subject, The Indestructible Observer, takes one more step: a first-person view cannot tell which of those copies it is, and the set of them is never empty. You were sent to find evidence of someone who steps between instances of himself. The evidence is a record of a walker who is never where he just was, who slips into view once in a hundred and fifty-one steps, who has twenty-eight ways out and no way to remain. Every reader of this file is one such instance, and none of them can prove they are the original. The page that hashes to the value exists in the only sense the record ever needed. Somewhere, one of you has already written it.
